question: A 62-year-old man comes to the physician because of painless swelling in his left foot for 4 months. The swelling was initially accompanied by redness, which has since resolved. He has not had fever or chills. He has a history of coronary artery disease, hyperlipidemia, and type 2 diabetes mellitus. He has had 3 sexual partners over the past year and uses condoms inconsistently. His mother had rheumatoid arthritis. Current medications include clopidogrel, aspirin, metoprolol, losartan, atorvastatin, and insulin. He is 180 cm (5 ft 11 in) tall and weighs 95 kg (209 lb); BMI is 29 kg/m2. Vital signs are within normal limits. Cardiovascular examination shows no abnormalities. Examination of the feet shows swelling of the left ankle with collapse of the midfoot arch and prominent malleoli. There is no redness or warmth. There is a small, dry ulcer on the left plantar surface of the 2nd metatarsal. Monofilament testing shows decreased sensation along both feet up to the shins bilaterally. His gait is normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Painless swelling in left foot" -> "Redness initially present" -> "Resolved redness" -> "Swelling persists" -> "History of coronary artery disease, hyperlipidemia, and type 2 diabetes mellitus" -> "Decreased sensation along both feet" -> "Small dry ulcer on left plantar surface of 2nd metatarsal" -> "Collapse of midfoot arch and prominent malleoli" -> "Diabetic arthropathy" -> 95%
analysis: The most likely diagnosis in this case is diabetic arthropathy, also known as Charcot arthropathy. The patient's history of type 2 diabetes mellitus, sensory neuropathy as evidenced by decreased sensation on monofilament testing, and the presence of a small dry ulcer on the foot are all consistent with this condition. The collapse of the midfoot arch and prominent malleoli are also characteristic findings of Charcot arthropathy.
